verses.translation_literal: Praise Yah! O the happinesses of a man fearing [obj] YHWH, in his commandments he delights exceedingly.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hallelujah. Praise Yah! Happy the one who stands in awe of the LORD, who finds in his commands not a burden but a delight, and a deep one.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens with the shout hallelu-yah, 'praise Yah': a plural command, a crowd called to its feet, with Yah the short form of the divine name. The KJV's 'Praise ye the Lord' swallows the name; the Hebrew has it. Then the voice turns from the crowd to one man, and the rest of the poem is a portrait of him.

The key word is 'ashrei, which is not a wish but an exclamation: 'oh, the happiness of!' (Young's Literal Translation has it right with 'O the happiness of'). The KJV 'Blessed is the man' makes it sound like a ruling handed down; the Hebrew is closer to a congratulation, and it is a different word from the 'blessed' of verse 2 (yevorakh, from barakh). 'Fearing' here is awe before a king, not terror, and the verse proves it in its second half: this man does not merely obey the commands, he takes pleasure in them (chafetz, 'delights'). The closing 'me'od', 'exceedingly', is the last word on the line, so the voice should lean on it. Ibn Ezra and Radak hear the delight as the opposite of obedience done for show. The KJV 'that delighteth greatly' is accurate; its relative 'that' is a smoothing, since Hebrew simply sets the clauses side by side. A word on staging: the first half-line starts with aleph and the second with bet. The poem is an alphabet.

philological_notes.note: A plural imperative 'praise!' plus Yah, the short form of the divine name. It frames the psalm as liturgy: the poem begins with a call to a congregation, then speaks about one person. Translations that turn it into 'Praise the Lord' lose the name.
A plural construct exclamation, 'the happinesses of', frozen as 'oh, how happy'. It congratulates; it does not pronounce a blessing the way barukh does.

'Fears' with the direct-object marker, not 'fears from'. Malbim reads the construction as awe of YHWH's majesty rather than dread of punishment, and cites the saying 'in his commandments, not in the reward of his commandments'.

verses.translation_literal: Mighty in the land will be his seed; the generation of the upright will be blessed.
verses.translation_dramatic: Mighty in the land his children will be, a whole generation of the upright, and blessing will rest on every one of them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The reward comes forward in the line before the man's own wealth does: it is his seed. Zera', 'seed', is the ordinary word for descendants, and in a world with no pensions it names the only security a man has. 'Mighty' is gibbor, the word for a warrior or a man of standing, and 'in the land' puts the strength in the public field of honor and not in a private estate. The KJV 'mighty upon earth' is a loose reading; 'ha-aretz' is the land, which in a psalm of Israel means this land.

The second half widens from the family to 'the generation of the upright', and 'it will be blessed' is a passive verb with no stated blesser: God is understood, not named. Ibn Ezra reads 'generation' as father and son together, Malbim as both worlds; the line is open to both. Play the second half as a promise that does not need to be proved on stage.

philological_notes.note: Mighty, strong; the word for a hero or warrior. Ibn Ezra notes that a 'k-' is missing, 'mighty [like a mighty man]', so that his children's standing is like that of a famous champion. Meiri reads it as physical strength or health.
'A generation of upright ones'. The construct phrase reads as the line of the upright as a class, not one cohort.

verses.translation_literal: Wealth and riches [are] in his house, and his righteousness [is] standing for ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: Wealth and riches fill his house, and his righteousness stands, standing still when all the rest has passed.
verses.directors_commentary:
'In his house' means the household in the old sense: family, servants, storerooms and flocks, the whole unit by which a man was measured. Hon and 'osher are near-synonyms, a pair, 'wealth and riches', that the speaker piles up to make the house sound full. The KJV 'shall be' turns a plain nominal clause into a prophecy; the Hebrew has no verb. It is a description of how things are.

Then the line turns on 'his righteousness'. Tzedaqah here is both his right conduct and, as the psalm goes on to show (verse 9), his giving. The participle 'omedet is 'standing', the same word that will return in verse 9. The KJV 'endureth' is fine in sense but loses the picture of a thing standing upright when everything else falls. The commentators divide about whether this is an eternal reward in the world to come (Radak, Metzudat David) or a lasting name here and in his children's lives (Radak's alternative); the Hebrew 'la-'ad' will bear both. The opposition the line draws, between wealth that sits in a house and righteousness that stands for ever, is the point.

philological_notes.note: A feminine participle, 'standing', agreeing with 'righteousness'. The same word in verse 9 repeats the line verbatim, so the poem names the righteousness twice as the thing that stays.
A pair of near-synonyms for property and riches. Malbim distinguishes them: hon is wealth one has, 'osher is the ability to enjoy it, which God must grant.

verses.translation_literal: It rises in the darkness, light, for the upright: gracious and compassionate and righteous.
verses.translation_dramatic: In the dark a light comes up for the upright, light rising where there was none. Gracious. Compassionate. Righteous.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the ambiguous line of the psalm. The verb zarach is the verb for a sunrise, a light that comes up over the horizon, and it is used here of light breaking into darkness. The Hebrew order is 'it rises in the darkness, light': the verb and the dark come first, the light arrives last, which is how dawn arrives. The KJV 'there ariseth' adds a dummy 'there' but keeps the order's effect.

Then three words with no subject: 'gracious and compassionate and righteous'. The KJV and ASV put in 'he is', and the BBE does too, deciding that God is meant. That is a choice, not a translation. These three adjectives (channun, rachum, tzaddiq) are the stock description of YHWH, as in the psalm just before this one, and Rashi's midrash and Meiri's both hear God himself becoming the light, as in 'the LORD is my light' (Psalm 27:1). But Radak admits the other reading: the upright man who learned these qualities from his Maker. The Hebrew can be said so that either hearer takes it, and the actor should not resolve it. Darkness is trouble, as Ibn Ezra and Radak say, and light is relief: it is not an abstract blessing but the moment when a hard night ends.

philological_notes.note: To rise, of the sun or of a skin-light; the verb of sunrise. Rashi takes it as transitive, 'he makes light rise' (hizrich). Meiri also reads a transitive perfect in the place of a future.
Two of the three are the covenant-name attributes of YHWH (Exodus 34:6); here 'righteous' is added. The grammar does not say who the subject is: God, or the upright man, or both.

verses.translation_literal: Good [is] the man showing favor and lending; he sustains his affairs with justice.
verses.translation_dramatic: Good is the man who is generous and who lends, and who holds his affairs steady by what is right.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Good' (tov) opens the line, and the Hebrew sets it before the man: 'good, the man who...'. The KJV's 'a good man sheweth favour' makes goodness the man's character; the Hebrew is closer to the exclamation of verse 1, 'it goes well with the man who...'. Chonen is 'shows favor', the verb of grace, the same root as 'gracious' in the line before. The man is imitating what God is.

Note the pairing: 'shows favor and lends'. In Israel a loan to a poor neighbour was an act of grace, not business, and carried no interest (Exodus 22:24); Radak says the loan goes to the poor who are too proud to accept a gift. The second half is where the KJV, 'he will guide his affairs with discretion', departs furthest from the Hebrew without being wrong. 'Guide' follows Rashi, who glosses yekhalkel as manhig, 'directs', and 'discretion' is an interpretive rendering of mishpat in the sense Radak and Meiri give it: right measure, the balance that keeps the giver from his own ruin. That is a defensible reading, and it is the one the commentators spend their time on. What the KJV loses is the plainer picture. Yekhalkel is 'sustains', 'supplies', the verb for provisioning a household or a king's table (Metzudat Zion cites 1 Kings 4:7), so the line says he keeps his own affairs supplied and standing. And mishpat is 'justice', the ordinary word for right order, which the KJV drops: the man's dealings are held to a standard, not merely to prudence. The dramatic line can carry both senses, as the commentators do: generosity that does not turn into his own ruin, and dealings that are fair to everyone.

philological_notes.note: A polel of kul, 'to contain, hold': to sustain, supply, provide for. Metzudat Zion compares 'they provided for the king' (1 Kings 4:7). Rashi glosses it 'directs', which is the source of the KJV 'guide'.

'With justice', the standard word of right order. Radak and Meiri read it as a right measure that keeps the giver from his own ruin, which is the sense behind the KJV 'discretion'; Malbim as honesty toward others. The Hebrew carries both.

verses.translation_literal: For for ever he will not be shaken; for a memorial of perpetuity the righteous one will be.
verses.translation_dramatic: He will never be shaken, never. And when he is gone he will not be forgotten: the righteous is remembered for ever.
verses.directors_commentary:
The line is built on a repetition: 'for ever' (le'olam) in the first half, 'perpetuity' ('olam) in the second. The ancient ear hears the word twice in two heartbeats. The KJV avoids the echo with 'for ever' and 'everlasting'; keep it. 'Not be shaken' (yimmot) is an image of a house or a foot that does not slip. It is the same verb that Psalm 15 and Psalm 16 use of the man who stands securely. Radak reads it as a body and wealth that stay whole, Metzudat David as one who is not inclined to fall.

The second half moves to memory. Zeker is a 'memorial', the thing by which a name stays in a community: in a society without records, to be remembered is a kind of survival. 'The righteous' is now the headline word, and note that the KJV 'Surely' for ki, 'for', hides the logic: this is the reason the preceding lines were true. His giving (verse 5) is why nothing shakes him.

philological_notes.note: 'For a memorial of perpetuity': the righteous one becomes a remembered name, not just a person who lives on. Radak reads it as being remembered well even after death; Metzudat David also in the next world.

verses.translation_literal: Of evil news he will not be afraid; steady [is] his heart, trusting in YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: A messenger may come with evil news, and he will not flinch. His heart is set, fixed like a post, leaning on the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
Shemu'ah is a 'thing heard', a report, which in a world without telegraphs means a runner, a caravan rumor, a rider at the gate. The line imagines one news: a battle lost, a child sick, a creditor on the road. The KJV 'evil tidings' is fine and archaic; the point is that the man does not fear it before it arrives or after. The verb is the same one as in verse 1, yira': 'fears'. The man who fears YHWH does not fear bad news. The poem does that deliberately: one fear drives out the other.

Nachon is 'set', 'fixed', 'established': the word for a foundation that has been laid. The KJV 'fixed' is right. The heart is a place, a house with its footing in YHWH. Radak adds that the man does not trust his wealth, his troops or his friends, but only God. Malbim takes the verse to be about guilt: some men fear news because of what they have done, and this man has nothing to be afraid of. Both readings fit; the scene needs only a man who hears the news and does not move.

philological_notes.note: A niphal participle: set up, established, firm, as a foundation or a house is. Rashi glosses it 'faithful to his Maker'.
'A bad report', literally 'a thing heard'. Radak reads news of one's sons or relatives abroad or of enemies marching; Meiri news of plotting rivals.

verses.translation_literal: Propped up [is] his heart, he will not fear, until that he looks on his foes.
verses.translation_dramatic: His heart is held up, leaning, and he is not afraid, not until the day he looks his enemies in the face.
verses.directors_commentary:
Samukh is 'leaning, propped, supported', the picture of a heart resting its weight on something. It is the passive participle of the verb for laying a hand on an offering. Where verse 7 had a heart set like a foundation, this one has a heart that leans, which is how a tired man actually stands. The KJV 'established' repeats the previous verse's idea; the picture is different.

The tricky phrase is the last. The Hebrew says only 'until that he looks on (be-) his foes'. The KJV adds 'his desire upon', the ASV the same, the BBE 'till he sees trouble come on his haters'. These are all readings: they hear the idiom as seeing the enemy fall, as in 'my eye has looked on my enemies' (Psalm 54:7). Meiri and Radak agree. Metzudat David offers a second thought: a frightened man could not look at his enemies' downfall at all. Notice what 'until' does: it does not say fear arrives at that point. It says the man is unafraid up to the moment of vindication, so the line is a statement about duration, and the stage moment is the staring across at the foe. Do not play it as gloating; the Hebrew does not.

philological_notes.note: A passive participle, 'supported, propped, leaned on'. Rashi: leaning on the Holy One. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'leaning'.
'Looks on his foes' with the preposition be-: to look at with satisfaction or in triumph. The English versions that supply 'his desire' supply what the idiom implies; the Hebrew does not say it.

verses.translation_literal: He scatters, he gives to the needy; his righteousness [is] standing for ever; his horn will be lifted up in honor.
verses.translation_dramatic: He scatters it, he gives it away, open-handed to the poor. His righteousness stands for ever, and his horn is lifted high in honor.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two verbs, no objects: 'he scatters, he gives'. Ibn Ezra notes that the object is left out because the word 'to the needy' makes it plain. Pizzar means to scatter or disperse, and a person who does it with money is both generous and unafraid; the Targum makes the object explicit, 'he scattered his money' (badar mamonei). On stage, a hand flung open like a sower's is a fair image for the actor, but it is a staging image, not the word's own picture. The KJV 'dispersed' is accurate but sounds like a council; 'he scatters' is what the word does. The poor are 'evyonim, the needy, those who have nothing to fall back on. Radak says the scattering means giving 'to this one and that one', to every needy person who comes before him; Radak and Meiri both stress that he does not give away everything and ruin himself, since a little to many is the virtue (Radak cites the rule that a giver should not give more than a fifth).

The second half repeats 'his righteousness is standing for ever' word for word from verse 3. Verse 3 told us the wealth in his house; now we know where the wealth went. The horn is the symbol of an animal's strength, and a lifted horn is a head held up: dignity. The KJV 'exalted with honour' is correct and no softening. Contrast the wicked's horn, cut off, as Radak notes with 'all the horns of the wicked I will cut off' (Psalm 75:11 in the Hebrew numbering).

philological_notes.note: To scatter or disperse, here of money given away in every direction. Radak glosses it as giving 'to this one and that one and to all the needy', a little to each, not ruin. The Targum renders it 'scattered his money'.
'His horn': the horn of a wild ox or ram stands for power and standing. Radak and Metzudat Zion gloss it as strength and rule.

verses.translation_literal: [The] wicked one sees and is vexed; his teeth he gnashes and melts away; the desire of [the] wicked will perish.
verses.translation_dramatic: The wicked man looks on, and it eats at him. He grinds his teeth, and he wastes away, and the thing the wicked long for comes to nothing.
verses.directors_commentary:
The camera swings to the outsider. After nine verses of the upright, the wicked appear in a single line, and the verbs are quick and physical: he sees, he is angry, his teeth grind, he dissolves. The wicked is seeing the man of verse 9, his open hand and his lifted horn. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat David all take it as envy.

The KJV 'be grieved' is a softening: ka'as is anger, vexation, the same root as the verb for provoking God. The wicked man is not sad; he is furious at what he sees. 'Gnash his teeth' is the plain Hebrew and the KJV keeps it. Nanamas, 'melts away', is the same image as wax or snow, a man losing his substance, and Radak reads it as his heart giving way. The last clause is the verdict: ta'avat, the 'desire' of the wicked, the thing they crave, will be lost. The last word, tovedh, 'will perish', is the psalm's final verb: what began with 'happy' ends with 'perishes'. Verses 9 and 10 are the longer ones, three letters each in the acrostic, as Radak and Meiri note.

philological_notes.note: To be vexed, angry, provoked. Rashi takes it as an active verb like 'and he was angry' (va-yikhas), and explains the half-qamets, half-patach pointing and the low accent on that basis.
To gnash the teeth, a gesture of rage. Metzudat Zion cites Lamentations 2:16 for the same verb.
'The desire of the wicked will perish': what they long for is lost. Radak reads it as the wish to see the righteous fall, which they will not see.
